sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Real-world observations are noisy and often contain excessive task-irrelevant information. Effective world modeling and planning need to abstract observations into world state representations while filtering out irrelevant information. However, encoders in existing world models are typically non-adaptive, leading to state representations that are easily distracted by task-irrelevant information. As a result, the model may not selectively filter observations to cater to different task demands. To address this problem, we introduce ConfigWM, which realizes configurable perception through task-conditioned state extraction. Given a language description of the task at hand, ConfigWM uses it as a configuration signal to steer how visual embeddings are mapped into a task-specific state space, selectively preserving information relevant to the current task while suppressing task-irrelevant variations. Action-conditioned dynamics are then learned in this task-specific state space for planning. We evaluate ConfigWM in environments with increasing levels of distraction. While existing methods exhibit substantial declines in planning success rate as the environments become increasingly noisy, ConfigWM remains comparatively stable and outperforms the strongest competing method by 22.3% on average across diverse environments. Consistent gains in physical-quantity probing (+0.365 Pearson r) and distracted-to-clean retrieval (+75.5%) further indicate that ConfigWM learns states that preserve task-relevant information while remaining robust to distractors, supporting reliable world modeling and planning in noisy worlds. Project Page: https://configwm.github.io

sections.title:
1 Introduction
Real-world environments contain far more information
and dynamics than are needed for any single task [Chen
et al., 2025b, Bharadhwaj et al., 2022, Toso et al., 2026].
However, what constitutes a sufficient state depends on
the task: different tasks may require different informa-
tion from the same observation. This challenge becomes
particularly pronounced in dynamic environments, where
multiple objects or agents may coexist and evolve simul-
taneously [Wu et al., 2026, Wang et al., 2026b]. In such
settings, only some of these dynamics may be relevant to
the current task. If task-irrelevant dynamics are retained
in the state, the world model must account for transitions
that do not contribute to the current objective, making
prediction and planning inevitably difficult.
sections.content: Existing world models do not explicitly resolve this challenge. In particular, feature-based world models construct states from task-agnostic representations [Zhou et al., 2024, Assran et al., 2025, Baldassarre et al., 2025]. However, desirable state should act as an information bottleneck, retaining only the information sufficient for current task while suppressing the task-irrelevant information [Pacelli and Majumdar, 2019, Eftekhar et al., 2024, Cui et al., 2026]. This is difficult to achieve with task-agnostic methods, since the relevance of an object can change with the task: the same object may be the target under one instruction but distractor under another. The same observation can Figure 1. ConfigWM Architecture. therefore require different representations under different task queries, whereas task-agnostic state representations remain unchanged. In the literature, it has also be noted that task-agnostic approaches may retain both target and distractor dynamics in the state [Nikulin et al., 2026]. These limitations motivate adapting representations to better preserve task-relevant information. more direct alternative is to introduce task conditioning directly into perception. This motivates configurable perception [LeCun et al., 2022, Shi et al., 2023, Marza et al., 2024], where the current task configures visual encoding to construct task-relevant state. In this work, we introduce configurable perception into World Models with Configurable Perception Sec 1: Intro Sec 2: Related Works Sec 3: Noisy Worlds Sec 4: Method Sec 5: Experiments Sec 6: Scaling Sec 7: Conclusion Sec 8: Appx world modeling and propose Config World Model (ConfigWM), an action-conditioned world model built on the task-relevant state abstractions, as illustrated in Fig. 1. Inspired by VL-JEPA [Chen et al., 2025a], we build ConfigWM on configurable encoder that steers visual prediction with task query and is therefore naturally suited to realizing configurable perception. The resulting query-conditioned representations define the task-relevant state space, over which ConfigWM learns action-conditioned dynamics for planning. To evaluate whether configurable perception improves world modeling under dynamic distraction, we augment Two-Room, Push-T, and OGBench-Cube [Maes et al., 2026a] with increasing numbers of dynamic, target-like distractors and conduct controlled comparisons across different training and testing conditions. Baseline methods degrade substantially when trained on clean observations and evaluated under distraction. More importantly, simply exposing them to distractors during training does not solve the problem and can even further impair planning performance. In contrast, ConfigWM remains consistently robust as distraction increases, with an average planning improvement of 22.3%. These results show that robustness does not arise merely from exposure to distractors during training. Rather, conditioning perception on the task allows the world model to selectively preserve taskrelevant dynamics while suppressing irrelevant motion, thereby supporting reliable prediction and planning in dynamically distracting environments. Apart from planning success, we further characterize the quality of the learned states from two complementary perspectives. Physical-quantity probing [Maes et al., 2026b, Alain and Bengio, 2016] measures how well the representations preserve task-relevant physical information, while distracted-to-clean retrieval [Garrido et al., 2024] evaluates their robustness to dynamic distractors. Across both analyses, baseline representations are increasingly affected as distractors are introduced, whereas ConfigWM remains substantially more stable. These results indicate that ConfigWM better preserves task-relevant information while suppressing noise. In summary, the contributions of this paper are as follows: We propose ConfigWM, which realizes configurable perception by using task instructions to construct taskrelevant latent states and learn action-conditioned dynamics over them. We augment Two-Room, Push-T, and OGBench-Cube with progressively increasing dynamic, target-like distractors, establishing controlled evaluation setting for world models in noisy environments. We show that ConfigWM maintains stable planning under dynamic distractors and achieves consistent gains in physical-quantity probing and distractedto-clean retrieval, indicating better preservation of task-relevant information.

sections.title:
2 Related Works
World State Representations. Recent world models have
explored several ways to obtain latent states suitable for
prediction and planning, from directly reusing pretrained
visual features to jointly learning or further adapting the
state representation. A common approach is to build pre-
dictive dynamics directly over pretrained or frozen visual
features, using these representations as the state space for
world modeling and planning [Zhou et al., 2024, Assran
et al., 2025]. Rather than fixing this state space, other ap-
proaches further shape the representation for downstream
control. Some jointly learn the latent state with dynamics,
reward prediction, and value-learning objectives, allowing
task returns to directly influence the learned representa-
tion [Hansen et al., 2022], others improve predictive state
learning through latent regularization [Maes et al., 2026b,
Zhao et al., 2026, Terver et al., 2026], explicitly ground
the latent space in physical state and motion [Yan et al.,
2026], or map generic visual features into more compact
and control-relevant representations [Wang et al., 2026a,
Fu et al., 2026a, Toso et al., 2026]. Compact latent represen-
tations have also been explored to improve the efficiency
of predictive planning [Yao et al., 2026]. Despite these ad-
vances, task relevance is typically introduced by shaping
the learned state, rather than by allowing the current task
to determine what visual information is encoded in the
first place.
sections.content: Steerable Representations. Recent work has explored visual representations that can be steered by task or language signals, allowing the same observation to produce different representations depending on the current query. Some methods condition the visual encoder directly, enabling its features to emphasize queried objects, regions, or attributes [Ruthardt et al., 2026, Mao et al., 2026], while others introduce textual conditioning into predictive representation learning, where the query guides the features being predicted [Huang et al., 2026, Chen et al., 2025a]. However, these methods primarily focus on learning taskconditioned visual representations, leaving open whether the resulting representations can support better actionconditioned world modeling and therefore improve downstream planning. Language has also been used to condition future prediction and action generation [Cheang et al., 2024, Brohan et al., 2023]. ConfigWM differs by applying language at the state construction stage to obtain the task-relevant states for planning, extending the steerable representations to action-conditioned world modeling. 2 World Models with Configurable Perception Sec 1: Intro Sec 2: Related Works Sec 3: Noisy Worlds Sec 4: Method Sec 5: Experiments Sec 6: Scaling Sec 7: Conclusion Sec 8: Appx Figure 2. sections.title:
3 Constructing Noisy Worlds
To evaluate world models under dynamic distraction, we
construct controlled noisy variants of three widely used
visual control environments: Two-Room [Sobal et al., 2025],
Push-T [Chi et al., 2025], and OGBench-Cube [Park et al.,
2025]. Together, they span 2D navigation, planar object
manipulation, and 3D robotic manipulation, covering
representative goal-conditioned planning settings studied
in recent latent world models [Zhou et al., 2024, Wang
et al., 2026a, Maes et al., 2026b].
sections.content: Unlike existing noisy settings that primarily modify background appearance or introduce static clutter [Pumacay et al., 2024, Rasouli et al., 2025], we introduce multiple dynamic, target-like distractors that move independently and compete with the real target, while preserving the original task and target motion. By progressively increasing the number of such distractors, we create nine difficulty levels for each environment, allowing us to systematically vary dynamic distraction without changing the underlying control problem. The resulting matched clean and noisy observations are also used as training pairs for configurable perception in our model. We next describe the distractor construction ( 3.1) and its instantiation in the three environments ( 3.2). 3.1 Dynamic Distractor Construction We construct the dynamic distractors directly in the observation space, without modifying the underlying simulator state or task dynamics. We first use SAM 3 [Carion et al., 2025] to segment and track the target-like objects from valid task rollouts. The extracted object masks are recolored and composited onto another rollout while preserving their original trajectories, producing visually similar objects whose motion remains consistent with the environment but is unrelated to the current task. Since this procedure operates only on the visual observations, it can also be adapted to other environments without modifying their underlying simulators. As illustrated in Fig. 2, each clean rollout is used to construct nine matched visual conditions. The zerodistractor condition 𝑑0 contains no additional distractors, while 𝑑ℓ contains ℓ independently moving distractors for ℓ = 1, . . . , 8. All levels share the same task query, action sequence, goal, and target trajectory, and differ only in the amount of competing object motion. Consequently, every noisy observation has paired clean observation from the same rollout and time step. This matched construction provides both controlled difficulty axis for studying world models under increasing distraction and the noisyclean pairs used to train the configurable encoder in Sec. 4.1. 3.2 Environment Instantiations Two-Room [Sobal et al., 2025]. continuous 2D navigation task in which an agent must move through two connected rooms to reach target location. We introduce additional agents with similar appearance, creating competing object motion around the query-specified agent. Push-T [Chi et al., 2025]. planar object-pushing task in which circular pusher moves T-shaped block to target pose. We introduce additional recolored T-shaped blocks, requiring the model to distinguish and track the queryspecified block among visually similar moving objects. OGBench-Cube [Park et al., 2025]. 3D robotic manipulation task in which robotic arm moves designated cube to target location. We recolor the robot arms in complete manipulation scenes and combine these scenes into tiled observation. This creates multiple simultaneous armcube interactions, while the task query identifies the scene relevant for prediction and planning.

sections.title:
5 Experiments
5.1 Experimental Setup
We compare ConfigWM with LeWM [Maes et al., 2026b],
TC-LeWM [Liu et al., 2026], Sub-JEPA [Zhao et al., 2026],
and EB-JEPA [Terver et al., 2026], with EB-JEPA evalu-
ated only on Two-Room following its official implemen-
tation. These methods retain their original state-learning
objectives and regularization strategies. To ensure a fair
comparison and isolate the role of configurable encoder,
ConfigWM uses the frozen configurable encoder to con-
struct query-conditioned predictive states while adopting
the LeWM-style action-conditioned causal Transformer as
its dynamics model. A trainable state projector maps the
spatial encoder features into the 192-dimensional global
state required by the dynamics model.
sections.content: We additionally construct DINOv2-WM as controlled encoder baseline. It replaces configurable encoder with frozen DINOv2 encoder while retaining an identical projector architecture, dynamics model, training objective, and planning protocol. Therefore, the comparison between DINOv2-WM and ConfigWM changes only how the visual predictive state is constructed. We also report Unified ConfigWM, which uses single configurable en5 coder jointly trained on pooled data from all environments and distractor levels. With this encoder frozen, separate world models are trained under the same per-environment training and evaluation protocol as the standard comparisons. All methods are trained on the same transition data and evaluated under the same planning protocol. Further optimization and evaluation details are provided in Appx. B. 5.2 Planning under Dynamic Distractors We first examine whether world models trained in clean environments can generalize to dynamic distractors. As shown in Fig. 13, when models trained on 𝑑0 are evaluated on 𝑑1𝑑8, the planning performance of all baselines decreases substantially as the distractor level increases. This result shows that predictive states learned in clean scenes do not readily generalize when multiple target-like objects introduce unseen competing motion. We further consider the matched setting, where each model is trained and evaluated at the same distractor level (𝑑𝑘 𝑑𝑘). As shown in Fig. 5, even level-matched training does not reliably recover planning performance across baselines, particularly at higher distractor levels. In contrast, ConfigWM consistently outperforms all competing baselines across distracted levels in all three environments. Beyond its consistent performance gains, ConfigWM exhibits substantially greater robustness to increasing distraction. At 𝑑8, it retains an average of 83.8% of its 𝑑0 success rate across the three environments, whereas the baselines retain only 42.0%. Notably, ConfigWM remains robust under distraction even when its dynamics model is trained only on 𝑑0 transitions, achieving performance comparable to its level-matched training. Full results are provided in Appx. C.1. These results suggest that training on distracted observations alone is not sufficient. When multiple visually similar objects exhibit valid task dynamics, existing world models struggle to identify which dynamics are relevant to the current task. By using the task query to configure perception, ConfigWM selects task-relevant predictive states before dynamics modeling and thereby achieves more robust planning under dynamic distractors. At each distractor level, we train linear probe on the frozen representations and report the macro-average Pearson correlation 𝑟 across the physical quantities defined for each environment [Maes et al., 2026b]. Fig. 6 summarizes the results, while quantity-wise probing results are provided in Appx. C.2. ConfigWM consistently preserves the linearly recoverable physical information as distractor difficulty increases. From 𝑑0 to 𝑑8, its probing score decreases by only 0.005 on average across the three environments, compared with an average decrease of 0.497 for the baselines in each environment. This contrast suggests that the query-configured predictive states preserve the task-relevant physical information even in the presence of multiple dynamic and target-like distractors. 5.4 Do Distracted Representations Align with Clean Counterparts? To examine whether the task query determines which visual information is retained in the predictive state, we freeze the configurable encoder and train single shared ViT decoder [Terver et al., 2025] on its predictor outputs. As shown in Fig. 7, changing only the queried color produces distinct reconstructions from the same input observation. Each decoded observation retains the queried block together with the task-relevant agent and target pose, while largely suppressing the remaining distractors. Since the decoder has no direct access to the query, these differences provide qualitative evidence that the query configures which visual content is retained in the predictive state. 5.6 Does Perceptual Configuration Affect Planning? While the decoding results provide qualitative evidence that configurable encoder realizes configurable perception, we further examine whether this query-dependent state construction affects downstream planning. We keep the task, observations, model, and planning procedure fixed, but replace the correct query with the other valid but mismatched queries referring to other objects in the scene. We further examine whether these representation-level metrics provide meaningful intermediate measures of downstream planning performance using correlation analysis [Dong et al., 2026, Shen et al., 2025]. Within each environment, we compare the raw representation scores with matched planning success across the six methods evaluated in all three environments and distractor levels 𝑑1𝑑8, and report the corresponding Pearson 𝑟 and regression line. As shown in Fig. 9, both metrics are strongly associated with planning success. Across the three environments, physical-quantity probing and retrieval achieve average Pearson correlations of 0.89 and 0.89, respectively. These results suggest that preserving task-relevant physical information and alignment with clean counterparts provide informative intermediate measures of planning performance across methods and distractor levels.

sections.title: 6 Scaling the configurable encoder
sections.content: with real-world data We explore scalable training route that converts existing egocentric [Grauman et al., 2022, Damen et al., 2022], robot manipulation [Khazatsky et al., 2024, ONeill et al., 2024] and internet instructional video [Tang et al., 2019, Chen et al., 2026] data into supervision for configurable perception. Given clean observation and its task description, VLM generates editing prompts specifying reasonable but taskirrelevant objects, which are inserted into the observation using an image-editing model. The task-relevant scene content and task description remain unchanged, and the original observation serves as the clean target. The configurable encoder is then trained to predict the representation of the clean target from the noisy observation conditioned on the task description. Fig. 10 shows held-out PCA visualizations across DINOv2, DINOv3, V-JEPA 2.1, and LingBot-Vision. Complementary patch-level linear probing for distractor and task-relevant region prediction shows that the configurable encoder reduces distractor average precision (AP) by an average of 17.9 percentage points relative to the frozen backbones, while task-core AP remains nearly unchanged, indicating weaker responses to task-irrelevant objects while preserving task-relevant states. Full quantitative results and the evaluation protocol are provided in Appendix D. These results suggest that our encoder can benefit different visual backbones, providing practical route for scaling configurable perception to large real-world video datasets, without requiring manual annotation.

sections.title:
7 Conclusion
We introduced ConfigWM, an action-conditioned world
model that brings configurable perception into state con-
struction. Rather than modeling dynamics over a fixed
task-agnostic representation, ConfigWM uses the task
query to construct a task-relevant state and learns action-
conditioned dynamics over it. Across three environments
with increasing dynamic, target-like distractors, Con-
figWM maintains stronger planning performance than the
baselines, while representation analyses show that its states
preserve task-relevant physical information and remain
more consistent with their clean counterparts as distraction
increases. We further examine whether the query actu-
ally configures the learned state, finding that decoding the
states under different queries reveals different task-relevant
state representations, while replacing the correct query
with a mismatched one leads to a substantial drop in plan-
ning success. Beyond these controlled environments, re-
sults on real-world data suggest a promising path to scaling
the configurable encoder across different visual backbones.

We first describe the shared distractor-generation pipeline in Sec. A.1, then its environment-specific instantiations in Sec. A.2, and finally the resulting dataset scale in Sec. A.3. A.1 Dynamic Distractor Generation Object Extraction. For each environment, we begin with the official clean rollouts and use SAM3 [Carion et al., 2025] to identify the task-relevant target object. Specifically, SAM3 segments the object and tracks its mask consistently across frames, producing sequence of per-frame masks and image-space trajectories. These masks and tracks provide the spatial extent and motion information required to replay the extracted objects as distractors in other rollouts. We then reconstruct each extracted object to match the native appearance of the corresponding environment. This reconstruction preserves its characteristic geometry, boundary profile, and shading while allowing controlled recoloring. Finally, the reconstructed object is composited into recipient rollout by replaying its tracked donor trajectory frame by frame. Consequently, each distractor follows motion observed in valid rollout rather than being independently repositioned in every frame, resulting in temporally stable and visually plausible distractors. Progressive noise levels. We construct the noise levels cumulatively. The 𝑑0 condition contains only the recolored task-relevant objects and no additional distractors. For each trajectory, we sample eight donor trajectories and keep their identities and tracks fixed throughout the construction. Starting from 𝑑0, we add one additional donor trajectory at each noise level. This progressive construction enables controlled comparisons while keeping all previously introduced distractors unchanged. Color-balanced and query-conditioned targets. In this work, we use object color as concrete and easily controlled visual configuration attribute, although the formulation itself is not inherently restricted to color. For example, the Two-Room environment uses nine semantically named colors: red, blue, green, orange, purple, cyan, yellow, pink, and brown. To prevent the clean target from being associated with fixed appearance inherited from the original dataset, such as the red ball in Two-Room, we recolor the task-relevant core object and balance the nine colors across trajectories. At every noise level 𝑑ℓ , the core object and its ℓ distractors are assigned mutually distinct colors. In addition to the standard source-to-clean pairs derived from the official datasets, we construct same-source multi-query dataset from 𝑑8, which contains the complete set of one core object and eight distractors. At temporal stride of five, the same noisy observation is paired with nine color queries and nine corresponding query-selected clean targets. This construction provides direct realization of configurable perception, changing only the language query changes the desired target while keeping the source pixels fixed. Each target retains only the object or manipulation scene specified by the query (task-relevant) and removes the non-queried (task-irrelevant) distractors, while preserving task-relevant contextual elements (e.g., goals and interaction objects). A.2 Environment-Specific Construction Two-Room. The task-relevant object is the moving ball. SAM3 is used to extract and track balls from donor trajectories. Their soft, Gaussian-like appearance is reconstructed with the native style of the environment, recolored, and replayed along the extracted trajectories. The room walls, and other static geometry are preserved during compositing. Queries follow the template {color} ball, and the corresponding target contains only the queried ball in the matched clean room observation. Push-T. The task-relevant object is the movable T-shaped block, while the green T-shaped region and blue pusher provide task context. Additional T-block trajectories are extracted from valid donor rollouts. We reconstruct each donor with the geometry and edge appearance of the original T-block, recolor it, and replay it along its donor trajectory. Only the donor T-block is transferred, while the green goal and blue pusher are retained from the recipient observation. Natural occlusions between the pusher, selected T-block, distractors, and goal are preserved during compositing. Queries follow the template {color} block. OGBench-Cube. Each donor corresponds to complete armcube manipulation trajectory, identified by the color of its robot arm. SAM3 is used to extract and track the relevant manipulation content, after which the robot arm is reconstructed with an environment-matched appearance and recolored. The associated cube and interaction context are retained so that each donor remains coherent manipulation scene. To keep all manipulation scenes visible, we use an adaptive tiled layout: 𝑑1𝑑3 use 2 2 grid, whereas 𝑑4𝑑8 use 3 3 grid. We later extend the same training formulation to real-world visual data in Sec. D. Below, we describe the model architecture, the patch-wise contrastive objective, and the training data and optimization setup. Architecture. Both the input encoder 𝐸𝑋 and target encoder 𝐸𝑌 are initialized from pretrained DINOv2-S. All images are resized to 224 224 and processed using the standard DINOv2 preprocessing pipeline. Each image is encoded into one CLS token and 16 16 grid of 384-dimensional patch tokens. During the configurable encoder training, 𝐸𝑋 is optimized jointly with the predictor, whereas 𝐸𝑌 is kept as an independent frozen copy of DINOv2, providing fixed target representation space throughout training. The predictor 𝑃𝜃 consists of the first three Transformer layers of pretrained Llama-3.2-1B. trainable linear layer maps the 384-dimensional visual tokens to the Llama hidden dimension, while the task query is tokenized with the Llama tokenizer and padded or truncated to at most 32 tokens. The pretrained Llama token-embedding layer is kept frozen, whereas the Transformer layers and the visual input and output projections are trainable. The predictor processes the concatenation of the visual CLS and patch tokens with the query tokens, and its visual patch outputs are projected back to 384 dimensions, matching the dimensionality of the DINOv2 feature space. This provides common feature interface for the subsequent world-model experiments and facilitates controlled comparison with DINOv2-WM. The target encoder receives only the corresponding clean target image and does not take the task query as input. This keeps the target representation query-independent, requiring the predictive branch to use the query to select task-relevant visual information from the noisy observation. Training Data. The configurable encoder is trained using the noisy-world datasets described in Appendix A. Each training sample consists of noisy source observation, task query, and the corresponding clean target. We use source-clean pairs constructed across different distractor levels and additionally include same-source multi-query samples, where the same observation is paired with multiple valid queries and clean targets. These samples provide diverse query-conditioned training signals while preserving the same underlying visual state. The overall scale of the constructed training data is summarized in Table 1. Since the source and target observations are spatially aligned, each predicted patch is contrasted against target patches at the corresponding spatial location across the contrastive bank. Targets sharing the same query-conditioned target identity are treated as positives, whereas samesource samples associated with different queries remain negatives. To isolate the contribution of the configurable encoder under controlled comparison, we replace LeWMs end-to-end visual encoder with the frozen configured-state representation model while retaining its state dimensionality, causal Transformer 16 World Models with Configurable Perception Sec 1: Intro Sec 2: Related Works Sec 3: Noisy Worlds Sec 4: Method Sec 5: Experiments Sec 6: Scaling Sec 7: Conclusion Sec 8: Appx dynamics core, and training objective. Accordingly, trainable spatial projector aggregates the configurable encoders patch features into the 192-dimensional state 𝑆𝑞 𝑡 , matching the state dimensionality used by LeWM. The projector is shared across input observations and target observations, and trained jointly with the world model, while all the configurable encoder parameters remain frozen. The dynamics predictor is causal Transformer with AdaLN-zero action conditioning. During training, it takes three-state context sampled at intervals of Δ = 5 environment steps, with each state conditioned on the intervening Δ-step action block, and predicts the subsequent states using teacher forcing. Actions are normalized using the training-set statistics. As controlled encoder baseline for ConfigWM, DINOv2-WM replaces the configurable encoder with frozen pretrained DINOv2-S visual encoder [Oquab et al., 2023] and does not use language conditioning. Its patch-token features are mapped to the 192-dimensional state space using the same spatial projector as ConfigWM. Scaling the configurable encoder with Real-World Data To assess whether the configurable encoder extends beyond controlled environments, we conduct an additional representation-learning study using diverse real-world video data and four large visual backbones, demonstrating that the framework can be readily instantiated with range of widely used visual encoders. Real-World Data Construction. We draw candidate cases from task-annotated clips in public datasets spanning three domains: egocentric video (e.g., Ego4D [Grauman et al., 2022], Ego-Exo4D [Grauman et al., 2024], and EPIC-KITCHENS100 [Damen et al., 2022]), robotic manipulation (e.g., DROID [Khazatsky et al., 2024], Open X-Embodiment [ONeill et al., 2024], and RoboMind [Wu et al., 2024]), and instructional video (e.g., ActivityNet [Caba Heilbron et al., 2015], COIN [Tang et al., 2019], and FineGym [Shao et al., 2020]). For each case, we sample frames as the clean target observation and its task description as the query. To construct paired noisy and clean observations, we use task-conditioned distractor-synthesis pipeline based on VLM-guided image editing and differential quality control. Given clean observation and its task query, VLM (Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct [Bai et al., 2025]) identifies the task-critical entities and proposes one or two visually plausible but task-irrelevant objects. It then produces structured edit instruction specifying the appearance and placement of each addition, which is executed by an image-editing model (Qwen-Image-Edit-2511 [Wu et al., 2025]) to obtain the noisy input observation. second pass with Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct compares the edited and clean observations and rejects edits that alter task-relevant content or scene geometry. Training and Qualitative Evaluation. We retain the configurable encoder architecture and training objective described in Section B.1, and instantiate it with four large visual backbones: DINOv2-Giant [Oquab et al., 2023], DINOv3-7B [Siméoni et al., 2025], V-JEPA 2.1-Gigantic [Mur-Labadia et al., 2026], and LingBot-Vision-Giant [Fu et al., 2026b]. All variants produce 64 64 patch grid. We train each variant for 1000 steps on 8 NVIDIA A100 GPUs 5, weight decay of 0.05, 50 warm-up steps followed by cosine decay, global using AdamW with learning rate of 10 batch size of 32, BF16 precision, and gradient clipping at 1.0. For qualitative evaluation, we apply the trained models to held-out cases and visualize PCA projections of the frozen-backbone and our representations.
